abstract: Language models are increasingly used in text generation, decision support, and automated interaction, creating a need for localized, reversible, and selective control of their behavior. Activation steering demonstrates that internal interventions can alter the behavior of frozen models, but how to select and evaluate compact, multi-site control interfaces remains an open question. I introduce sparse internal control, a framework for steering target behavior by applying inference-time interventions to a small set of internal model nodes. A local target-controllability formulation characterizes candidate site–direction pairs by their behavioral effects and specifies constraints on target recovery, off-target preservation, and intervention energy. Two complementary selectors instantiate this formulation: Driver-OMP selects nodes for sparse reconstruction of a desired behavioral displacement, while Coverage-Driver favors stable coverage across prompts. I propose a six-axis control-evaluation protocol measuring reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse. Exploratory experiments on indirect object identification, MMLU multiple-choice question answering, sentiment steering, and refusal steering provide evidence for the feasibility of steering task-defined behavior through sparse internal interventions. The six-axis evaluation characterizes these interventions beyond target movement, revealing distinct control properties that depend on the task and available direction information. Together, the formulation, reference algorithms, and evaluation protocol provide a foundation for the systematic study and development of internal control methods for language models.

sections.body: The section motivates controlling frozen language models through a small set of internal variables under bounded intervention strength and limited collateral change. It contrasts this with parameter-changing methods such as RLHF, preference optimization, and model editing, and with external methods such as prompting and decoding. It places the work alongside mechanistic interpretability, activation steering, sparse autoencoder features, and representation editing. The contributions are a formulation of sparse internal control, two selection algorithms (Driver-OMP and Coverage-Driver), and a six-axis control-evaluation protocol. Figure 1 gives a conceptual illustration of the framework.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Frozen language models may be steered by sparse internal interventions, but selecting and evaluating such control interfaces is an open question.

sections.body: The section defines a frozen Transformer, a task-specific behavioral readout, a target-control set, and an off-target preservation set. Candidate control nodes are site-direction pairs with selection costs, and interventions are additive patches with coefficients `beta`. It defines weighted sparsity and an intervention energy, $E(\beta)=\beta^{\top}W\beta$. Definition 1 is an epsilon, delta, kappa control certificate requiring a normalized target residual at most `epsilon`, off-target loss at most `delta`, and energy at most `kappa`. The problem minimizes weighted sparsity plus a weighted energy term subject to this certificate. The formal solution uses a local linear approximation, support selection, strength refitting, and nonlinear evaluation.
sections.heading: Sparse internal control
sections.headline: Sparse internal control is formulated as selecting few site-direction interventions that meet target, preservation, and energy certificates.

sections.body: The procedure has three stages: local proposal, shared strength refit, and nonlinear evaluation in the original Transformer. Candidate effects are first-order terms `g_{i,v}` built from the Jacobian of the readout at each site. Driver-OMP adds candidates by regularized, cost-normalized residual alignment and refits strengths after each addition. With unit-normalized columns, unit costs, and no regularization, it reduces to ordinary orthogonal matching pursuit. Coverage-Driver adds candidates by marginal gain in saturated row coverage, so it favors rows that remain insufficiently covered. Both return a support and refitted strengths, which are then checked nonlinearly against the certificate conditions.
sections.heading: Driver-selection algorithms
sections.headline: Two selectors, Driver-OMP and Coverage-Driver, choose compact supports from a local linear approximation of the behavioral effects.

sections.body: The protocol evaluates an intervention at dose `gamma`, where `gamma` = 1 is nominal. Reachability is the normalized target residual at nominal dose. Signed reversal applies the negated patch to the target-side input and computes a ratio of distances to the target and source readouts. Dose response reports a progress measure and a signed Spearman rho over a dose grid. Feedback controllability adjusts only the dose to track a scalar target, reporting terminal error, hit rate, and evaluation counts. Off-target preservation uses KL divergence on non-target prompts. Held-out reuse tests refit-beta and frozen-beta conditions on prompts excluded from support selection. Thresholds are task-specific and adjustable.
sections.heading: Control evaluation protocol
sections.headline: A six-axis protocol measures reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback control, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse.

sections.body: Experiments cover IOI and Sentiment on GPT-2 small, MMLU Humanities and STEM on Qwen3-4B, and Refusal on Qwen3-1.7B, with all parameters frozen. Driver-OMP passes IOI nominal reachability in 10/10 seeds at epsilon 0.4 with mean 0.201 ± 0.058. Under evaluation-pair directions, IOI reversal passes on all three selectors in ten seeds, while fixed training-mean directions give 0/8 Sentiment reversal seeds. Feedback reaches 46/48 Humanities endpoints for Coverage-Driver under evaluation-pair directions, but only 7 to 8 of 48 MCQA endpoints under fixed directions. Mean off-target KL on the 32-prompt panel is high for Humanities, STEM, and Sentiment, with no seed passing. Refusal produces no reversal and no nominal reachability, though its dose curves are ordered.
sections.heading: Experiments: sparse internal variables as controllable actuators
sections.headline: Selected interventions reach targets and reverse behavior under paired-example directions but fail under fixed directions and preserve off-target behavior poorly.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the formulation, the two selectors, the nonlinear certificate, and the six-axis protocol. It reports that sparse supports can reduce task-defined readout errors, while nominal reachability depends on direction information. Coverage-Driver and Top-k meet the target criterion in every held-out MCQA and Sentiment evaluation-pair seed and no fixed-direction seed. Refusal shows ordered dose response without reachability or reversal. Fully frozen MCQA reuse remains weak and preservation shows substantial off-target distribution change. Suggested future work includes learning direction rules that do not need paired contrasts, adding explicit preservation and energy constraints to practical algorithms, and extending to multi-token generation.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Sparse internal control is presented as a framework and evaluation protocol, with reachability depending on direction information and off-target preservation remaining weak.

sections.body: The appendix expands the problem definition, including the frozen computation graph, readouts, off-target sets, candidate libraries, patching, weighted sparsity, and intervention energy. Later sections cover assumptions and proofs for local linearization and energy-constrained refitting, pseudocode and complexity for `SharedRefit`, Driver-OMP, and Coverage-Driver, and the six evaluation axes. Further sections give task specifications, reference constants, and extended results on model scope and Refusal continuations. The limitations section notes that paired-direction results do not establish control without that information, and that preservation measures distribution change rather than semantic safety. The reproducibility section lists the code repository, hardware, and statistical reporting conventions.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix defines the problem, proofs, algorithms, evaluation axes, task settings, constants, extended results, limitations, and reproducibility records.
